Consider Silver Star as a warrior.

The power of mental contamination makes one person into a great disaster. Just now, leave that aside.

What makes her the strongest individual fighter is, first of all, gravitational flight. This one concerns us very much.

An ordinary warrior gets thrust from the Gattari, the barrels, and lift from the horo, the wings. Thus flight—Nail—becomes possible.

The fastest means of travel in humanity's possession.

Faster than every vehicle, every ship, every airship. So a warrior decides whether there will be a fight at all. The choice belongs to him. His main attacks are bodily ones also, turning all that speed into destructive force. Enough to fatally damage any weapon.

That is why warriors stand above every other arm. Kings of the battlefield.

Silver Star is king among warriors for the same sort of reason.

Ordinary warriors work the air with Gattari and horo to fly. Silver Star gives air a supporting role only. No air? She can still fly.

Those thin, faintly shining, fragile-looking wings do not entrust themselves to air. They use shinki. Gravity. Universal attraction.

One of nature's most fundamental forces.

Silver Star. Second Generation Uemon-no-jou Muramasa recognizes this force, grasps it, controls it. Gravity from surrounding objects, gravity from her own body—within the limit of the pilot's heat output, she can increase it, reduce it, change the direction in which it acts.

Ordinary flight and gravitational flight, therefore, are not playing in the same league.

For example—

The higher warrior had Earth's gravity on his side and charged with greater force. For the lower warrior it was the reverse: gravity opposed him, and he intercepted while losing force.

How great the difference became depended on the angle.

Roughly, the higher warrior's angle of descent and the lower warrior's angle of ascent could be considered directly proportional. Move that angle away from ninety degrees, and the gap in force diminished. Bring it toward ninety, and the gap opened, multiplying.

And just now, the angle was almost ninety degrees.

Eighty-nine, perhaps. Our horizontal distance and difference in altitude gave that result.

Not bad.

Silver Star in full condition would probably have made it eighty-nine point nine.

A drop in the bucket? I had decided to forget that expression.

...Whichever way I dressed it, nearly ninety degrees.

She would come almost vertically down. We would go almost vertically up. This arrangement was already settled.

Silver Star would attack from the stratosphere, with gravity helping to its utmost—and her own ability making that help greater still.

Momentum equals mass times velocity. What figure would we get?

...I stopped calculating halfway. Not because I had discovered enough energy to stack at least twenty Muramasas and break the lot like roof tiles, then lost heart. No, no.

There was no point finding the answer to begin with.

Enough energy to break the enemy's armor was enough. Beyond that, waste. Smash the whole armor beyond recognition, or cut a few inches into the neck and rupture the carotid artery. Same value.

Going against gravity, we had difficulty getting even the necessary energy by ourselves.

But the force of collision, naturally, was relative.

If Silver Star's dive had enough collision force to destroy us, our counter would get the same collision force. That was the reasoning.

She could destroy us. We could destroy her.

...Equal, then? Arre, not so fast.

Altitude meant advantage or disadvantage. Common knowledge in warrior combat. No reason to doubt it.

Two lumps of iron colliding, fine. Above, below, same thing. But warriors had hands, feet, weapons. They had to make an attack.

Gravity helped or hindered every one of those movements. The attack from above became quick and sharp. From below, heavy and slow. A large difference in precision.

The higher warrior could catch the enemy more easily, deliver sufficient force more easily. In short, less chance of making a mess of it. The lower warrior got the opposite facility.

A fight in the sky, already testing the limits of vision and reaction speed. The importance hardly needed explaining.

Equal collision force. Unequal attack power. Both statements could be true.

Either side could destroy the other. Their chances of actually doing it were different. Call it the proportion of relative energy successfully used in an attack, if you liked. Same matter.

That was the short version.

And if the attacks met squarely head-on, it became simpler still. The greater momentum blew the lesser away. A one-sided result, no further discussion.

A fight in the sky, already testing the limits of vision and reaction speed. The importance hardly needed explaining.

Equal collision force. Unequal attack power. Both statements could be true.

Either side could destroy the other. Their chances of actually doing it were different. Call it the proportion of relative energy successfully used in an attack, if you liked. Same matter.

That was the short version.

And if the attacks met squarely head-on, it became simpler still. The greater momentum blew the lesser away. A one-sided result, no further discussion.

Not a natural disaster. Not a meteorite.

She was beyond what one sword could answer.

Still, if I meant to defeat her by technique—

My own limit would have to be crossed also.

A tsurugi's radar was the quickest, most accurate means of detection. Only the tiniest delay—the time for its signal to return—and Muramasa would know Silver Star had begun the attack.

Earlier, I had trusted my eyes. Lost.

Radar, our ears, had the greater range. The information would certainly come sooner.

...Still too late. I knew it.

Muramasa probably knew also.

A grain of delay. Even that much was fatal. To win, I had to know earlier.

At the very instant Silver Star began—

No. That also was too late.

Before she began.

Know the moment of attack before the attack existed. Then, and only then, I could respond.

Against a charge approaching the speed of light, the one way was to go beyond time.

The moment of Sen. In the Yoshino style, the Principle of Darkness.

No supernatural powers required. What it required was observation. Fine, painstaking observation, like building a great tower one small stone at a time.

Not watching the attack. Reading the signs of it.

A slight movement of the eyes. A muscle tightening. From those things, know the attack before the movement began.

Press into that moment and crush the first move. That was seizing Sen, the Yoshino style's Principle of Darkness.

Against Silver Star, I could not do that. Physically impossible to stop her attack before it began.

But afterward, I could respond. Should be able to respond.

Use the moment of Sen to take Go-no-sen, perhaps. If I could know the dive was coming even one nanosecond earlier, I could meet it with my blade.

Perhaps both of us would die.

But I could bring her down.

攻撃開始を察知するだろう。

　<ruby>信号探査<rt>みみ</rt></ruby>は有効範囲の広さという点で確実に優れる。
確実に視覚より早く情報を掴むだろう。

　……だが、それでも間に合わないと悟っている。
　おそらくは村正も。

　ほんの僅かな、砂粒のようなタイムラグ、それだけ
の遅れさえも致命的なのだとわかっている。
　勝つには――もっと早く知らねばならない。

　銀星号が、攻撃を始めるその瞬間に……
　
　否。違う。<ruby>それでも<rt>・・・・</rt></ruby>間に合わない。

　攻撃を始める<ruby>よりも前に<rt>・・・・・</rt></ruby>。
　攻撃が実現するより先に、その開始の機を知らねば
ならない。そうして初めて対応が可能になる。

　<ruby>物理限界速度<rt>ヴェロシティ・オブ・ライト</rt></ruby>にも迫る突撃を破るのなら。
　<ruby>時間<rt>とき</rt></ruby>を越えるのが唯一の方途だ。

　<ruby>先<rt>セン</rt></ruby>の機、と云う。
　吉野御流においては無明の理と称する。

　これは<ruby>所謂<rt>いわゆる</rt></ruby>超能力に類する何かを要求するものでは
決してない。
　求められるのは小石を積んで巨塔を築くかのような
精細かつ入念な観察である。

　攻撃の動作を<ruby>見る<rt>・・</rt></ruby>のではなく。
　攻撃の兆候を<ruby>読む<rt>・・</rt></ruby>のだ。

　微妙な視線の移動。あるいは筋肉の緊張。
　そういった情報から、敵の攻撃動作が実際に始まる
よりも<ruby>先に<rt>・・</rt></ruby>それを悟る。

　その機に押して攻め、敵の出端を打ち伏せるのが先
の機を取るという事であり吉野御流は無明の理である
が、銀星号に対してそれは成し得ない。
　あの攻撃を発動前に制するのは物理的に不可能だ。

　が――発動後の対応はできる。できる筈だ。
　先の機を突いて<ruby>後の先<rt>ゴノセン</rt></ruby>を取る格好になろうか。降下
突撃の到来を<ruby>十億分の一秒<rt>ナノ・セカンド</rt></ruby>でも先に知ることがもしも
できたなら、迎撃の剣を<ruby>合わせられる<rt>・・・・・・</rt></ruby>。

　あるいは相討。
　しかし、斃せる。

Far overhead, the enemy.

Sharpen my warrior's sight as much as I liked, I could not see even a mustard-seed shape.

Eyes moving? Muscles tightening? Nothing to read.

But information could not end there.

Heat from skin. The smell of flesh. A heartbeat. Something small, somewhere, had to exist.

Or something finer still. Nothing sight, hearing, smell or touch could catch, yet something that spoke to all of them—

The wavelength of a life being there. Something like that.


There was.

Presence, people called it. Now I could feel it, without doubt.

At the far end of the sky.

Not because my senses had become so excellent. No credit to me.

The opposite. The presence was simply that enormous.

To know the enemy, watch the breathing.

Not the sound. Not the movement.

That tells you about the breath at the mouth only. Anyone can fake that if they want, no?

So read the skin's breathing.

That one cannot be faked. Nobody can lie with their skin.

Feel it with your own skin. Yours and the enemy's are connected by the air.

The skin's breathing reaches your skin. Read it there.

Breathing will tell you. Does the enemy mean to attack or defend? If attack, when?

Intent lies in the breath.

...Well. This is it, I suppose.

My own little secret of the art.
